alternatives.option: Require `Nullable<T>` for every nullable column, with no sentinels.
alternatives.whyRejected: It is verbose for Guid and floating-point fields, which commonly use Empty and NaN as "no value" in .NET code already.

alternatives.option: Always return a model, letting callers inspect key fields for emptiness.
alternatives.whyRejected: It pushes absent-record detection into every caller, and it is error-prone when a shard key is a non-nullable struct.

fields.consequences: Callers get null for absent records and can use non-nullable Guid and double properties naturally. A literal `Guid.Empty` or `NaN` cannot be stored through a non-nullable property. Because nested models are flattened, a required column inside one nulls the whole parent model. When a required null discards a model, the Mapper logs which column caused it at Debug level, because the resulting null carries no clue.
fields.context: Most columns can be null, but C# value types cannot. Some nulls are ordinary attribute values; others, such as a null primary key from an outer join or a not-found output parameter, mean there is no record at all. Returning an object with all-default properties in that case is a common source of bugs.
fields.decision: Database null maps as follows. Reference types (strings, arrays) map null to null. `Nullable<T>` value types and nullable enums map null to null. The non-nullable `Guid`, `double` and `float` use null sentinels: `Guid.Empty` and `NaN` read and write as database null, while their nullable forms store those values literally. Other non-nullable value types have no null representation. Separately, a mapping marked required makes a database null mean that the record is absent: the Mapper yields no model (null, or the row is omitted from a list) rather than a model with a null property. A non-nullable ShardKey property receiving null data is an error unless the mapping is required.
fields.title: Represent database null with nullable types, null sentinels and the required flag
